SK2062 A later condition in the chain repeats an earlier one

One if/else if chain tests the same side-effect-free condition twice, so the later branch is unreachable and the case it was written for is never handled.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS1862, S2760

Why

In an if/else if chain nothing at all runs between one condition and the next: reaching the second means the first was false, so a second condition identical to the first is false too and its body is dead. No compiler reports it, because the code is perfectly well formed — it simply does something other than what it looks like. ⚠ The comparison is structural, not textual. if (a && b) and if (b && a) are different conditions and neither is reported for the other; two conditions that merely share a sub-expression — if (x.Kind == A) … else if (x.Kind == B) — are different conditions too. Only a whole condition equal to a whole earlier condition, token for token and ignoring layout, is a finding.

Example

Instead of:

if (mode == Mode.Fast) { Fast(); } else if (mode == Mode.Fast) { Careful(); }

Write:

if (mode == Mode.Fast) { Fast(); } else if (mode == Mode.Careful) { Careful(); }

When it does not fire

⚠ Sequential `if` statements are deliberately not reported, and that is the rule's main exclusion. Two separate ifs testing the same thing are only pointless when nothing between them changed the answer, and the first body usually did exactly that — if (dirty) { Flush(); } if (dirty) { … } needs the bodies read before it means anything. Only conditions inside one if/else if chain, where no statement can run between the two tests, are compared. ⚠ The condition must be side-effect free: an invocation, an await, an assignment, an ++ or a -- anywhere in either condition withdraws the finding, because if (Read()) … else if (Read()) really is two different questions. ⚠ Structural equality, never text. SyntaxFactory.AreEquivalent compares the trees ignoring trivia, so layout, line breaks and comments do not decide it, and neither does a shared sub-expression: only complete conditions are compared with each other, never their parts. Element access is excluded because an indexer is a call. A condition containing a preprocessor directive is excluded, because the two branches of an #if are not the same program. ⚠ The side-effect test is asked once, of the later condition, and once is enough: IsRepeatable is a pure function of the syntax and the structural comparison compares the syntax, so two equal conditions always answer it the same way. A second copy of the guard was in the first draft and a sabotage proved no test could reach it. Every later condition is compared against every earlier one in its own chain and the finding points at the repeat, not at the original. There is no fix: which of the two conditions was meant to be something else, and what, is the entire content of the bug. Generated code is excluded.
